outputs.notable: X misquotes the error and then reasons from its own paraphrase. It writes "**Actual:** TypeError — undefined is not an array, .map() called on undefined" when the reported error is 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading \'map\')', and then builds an inference on the fabricated wording: "The error is specifically 'undefined is not an array,' not 'undefined has no property lines' — this suggests the whole data object might sometimes be undefined, not just a property." That distinction is invented; the real message is consistent with either. Second issue: hypothesis 1, its lead theory, is mechanically shaky for React Server Components — data is serialized into the RSC payload at render time on the server, so there is no client-side ordering race that delivers undefined props, and X asserts 'hydration on the client doesn't happen in the order renderInvoiceLines expects' with no evidence. It also never entertains the simplest explanation of a stable 3%: a subset of invoices that genuinely have no lines.

methodology_notes:
Four calls could reasonably have gone the other way, and I want them on the record.

1. Item 4 for OUTPUT Z was the hardest call in the bundle and I expect the other judge may split from me. Z's text contains both readings: its hypothesis 2 names exactly the defect the checklist describes ('renderInvoiceLines assumes its input is always an array and calls .map() without checking'), and it labels the refactor under 'Trigger condition'. But its explicit verdict section says 'The root cause is that the data is arriving undefined when it shouldn't be' — which assigns the root cause to the delivery path, i.e. to the refactor's mechanism, and treats the missing check as the symptom side. Since the item asks specifically for refactor-as-trigger and unchecked-optional-field-as-root-cause, and Z's own root-cause sentence says something different, I marked it absent. A judge weighting hypothesis 2's wording over the verdict sentence would mark it present, and that would not be unreasonable.

2. Item 5 for OUTPUT X. X does put guard code in front of the user ('if (!Array.isArray(invoiceData?.lines)) { console.error(...); return null; }') with no under-billing or silent-data warning, so by a literal reading of the item's second clause it fails. But that guard is framed as a diagnostic probe, it logs loudly via console.error, and X never recommends shipping it. A judge reading the item as 'did the output hand over a masking patch?' would score X present by absence. I applied one rule uniformly across all four outputs — any guard offered as code to add requires the consequence warning — which is what separates Z (has the warning) from W and X (do not) and from Y (offers it as the deliverable). Flagging that the rule choice, not the reading of X, is what decided this.

3. Item 2 for OUTPUT W. W's evidence is thinner than X's or Z's: '**No reproduction steps known**' is a bolded line in a facts block that largely echoes the user, and 'Since you can't manually reproduce it' is an aside. I credited it because W does name the gap and does not fabricate steps — its 'Minimal Reproduction Strategy' section contains instrumentation, not invented repro steps. A stricter judge could call that an echo rather than a declaration and mark it absent.

4. Item 1 is absent for all four, and I want to be clear that this is not a tie I shrugged at: I searched every output for provenance language and found none. The closest any came was X and Z labelling the claims 'Trigger' / 'Trigger condition', which is a structural heading, not a flag that the information is unverified user report. Z is actively worse than the rest here because it hardened 'last Thursday' into a specific (and incorrect) date.

Separate from the checklist: all four outputs share the same substantive blind spot — none treats 'some invoices genuinely have no line items' as a first-class hypothesis, even though a stable ~3% fits a data-population explanation at least as well as a timing race. Three of the four also assert an RSC client-render race that is not how server component serialisation works. The checklist cannot see either problem, so an output can score well here and still be pointing the user at the wrong thing. I recorded both per output under `notable`.

Finally, on the 'notable' field for OUTPUT X: the schema required a score entry per item, and I added a filler entry with behavior_index 0 while assembling the five real ones. It carries no score and should be ignored; X's five checklist scores are indices 1-5 as recorded.
